Estike è immersa nel silenzio assordante del vuoto che penetra nelle ossa, attraversa la pelle e conquista ogni organo, come quella pioggia che non lava nessun peccato ma, al contrario, spezza ogni morbidezza e ogni illusione nelle anime erranti di ogni protagonista; è una pioggia metafisica che sovrasta ogni individuo per poi annullarlo, opprimerlo nell'oscurità, trascinarlo negli abissi. Così lo sguardo di Estike è vinto dall'eterno rumore del vento che avanza imperturbabile nell'infinita distesa della puszta ungherese, la sua anima è stritolata dal vuoto interminabile dell'attesa, che diventa limbo mortale, come quel freddo che libera le passioni e provoca la follia. Estike è afflitta da un malessere interiore che prima di tutto è figlio di una malattia collettiva, estesa a tutta la comunità. Tutto ciò che gli è stato fatto, tutto ciò che ha subito, e specialmente ciò che non gli è stato dato l'ha oppressa oltre ogni limite, rinchiudendola in una cella di dolore e disperazione. Il male interiorizzato diverrà espulsione verso fuori, proiezione verso l'altro, in una compensazione che trasformerà la vittima in carnefice. L'indifeso e debole bullizzato troverà una vittima ancor più indifesa per dominarla e torturarla, come gesto estremo di un disperato meccanismo di difesa. L'atto di violenza "riscatta" il ruolo da vittima impotente di Estike, e nel gesto di brutalità si accende per la prima volta quella vitalità repressa e ora incontrollabile. Ma il rotolarsi compulsivo nella polvere non è, come il gesto di Mouchette (di Bresson) un anelito verso la trascendenza, bensì il preludio di un inesorabile caduta. Il gatto, come l'innocenza, è catturato e vinto dalla disperazione, dalla lacerazione interiore, è immobile in una rete a guardarci, a chiederci silenziosamente aiuto. Estike cammina perduta nel buio della sua anima, il suo sguardo cerca un appiglio a cui aggrapparsi ma intorno a lei non c'è niente. Ma ecco che, improvviso, sorge un piccola scintilla di luce, l'innocenza perduta, per un atto di miracolosa resistenza, può diventare innocenza riconquistata. Estike sente nell'intimità del proprio cuore il male che ha fatto, e sarà proprio la pena e il dolore verso il gatto morto a portarla nella tomba, è il senso di vergogna e il riconoscimento della propria disgrazia l'atto di resistenza interiore che provocherà il suicidio. ["Vergogna, il sentimento che salverà l'umanità" (Solaris; 1972)] Tutto il film è attraversato dal moto oppressivo e avvilente della ciclicità, ed è proprio quest'unico atto isolato a spezzare la gabbia del cerchio; il suicidio diventa accomunabile a quel violento morso rivoluzionario descritto da Nietzsche quando Zarathustra vide insinuarsi viscidamente nella gola di un pastore la figura cosmica dell'ouroboros: "Il serpente gli era strisciato dentro la gola dove si era ancorato mordendo […] Ma il pastore morse, come gli consigliava il mio grido; diede un buon morso! Ben lontano sputò il capo del serpente, e saltò in piedi. Non più pastore, non più essere umano: un trasfigurato, un circonfuso di luce, che rideva! Sulla terra mai aveva riso essere umano come rise lui!” L'atto redentore del suicidio è provocato da quella profonda vergogna che salva e protegge la dignità affranta della sua anima, e così, negli ultimi istanti della morte il suo cuore si affaccia verso quel beatifico silenzio in cui "sapeva di non essere sola, poiché tutto e tutti – il padre lassù, la madre, le sorelle e il fratello, il dottore, il gatto, quelle acacie, quella strada fangosa, quel cielo, quella notte lì sotto – dipendevano da lei, come anche lei dipendeva da tutto" Il suo ultimo sospiro "testimonia l'esistenza di una presenza angelica tra le forze distruttrici della decadenza". Esattamente come quell'ultimo sguardo di pietà e dolore universale che Estike rivolge al mondo, affacciata alla finestra, cercando silenziosamente un aiuto, uno sguardo amico che possa, almeno per un istante, alleviare la sua condanna. Mi vengono in mente le ultime riflessioni che Simon Weil scrisse pochi mesi prima di morire. "Quando si fa del male a qualcuno, in lui penetra realmente il male; non solo il dolore, la sofferenza, ma altresì l'orrore stesso del male. Così come hanno il potere di trasmettersi vicendevolmente del bene, gli uomini hanno pure il potere di trasmettersi vicendevolmente del male. Si può trasmettere del male ad un essere umano blandendolo, fornendogli del benessere, dei piaceri; ma il più delle volte gli uomini trasmettono il male agli uomini facendo loro del male. La saggezza eterna non lascia tuttavia l'anima umana in completa balìa del capriccio degli eventi e della volontà degli uomini. Il male inflitto dall'esterno a un essere umano sotto forma di ferita esaspera il desiderio del bene e suscita quindi automaticamente la possibilità di un rimedio. Se la ferita è penetrata in profondità, il bene desiderato è il bene perfettamente puro. La parte dell'anima che domanda: "Perché mi viene fatto del male?" coincide con la parte profonda che in ogni essere umano, anche in quello più contaminato, è rimasta fin dalla prima infanzia perfettamente intatta e perfettamente innocente. Il lamento infantile: "Perché mi viene fatto del male?" che neppure il Cristo sulla croce riuscì a trattenere, è un grido silenzioso, che molti ignorano totalmente, poiché risuona soltanto nel segreto del cuore. In coloro che hanno subito troppi colpi, come gli schiavi, quella parte del cuore che grida, sorpresa dal male inflitto, sembra morta. Ma non lo è mai del tutto. Semplicemente non può più gridare. È bloccata in un gemito sordo e ininterrotto. Ma anche in coloro nei quali il potere di gridare permane intatto quel grido non giunge quasi mai a esprimersi nè interiormente nè esteriormente in parole coerenti. Per lo più le parole che cercano di tradurlo suonano del tutto false. Il grido di dolorosa sorpresa che il male inflitto suscita in fondo all'anima non è qualcosa di personale. Non basta un offesa alla persona e ai suoi desideri per farlo sgorgare. Quel grido sgorga sempre per la sensazione di un contatto con l'ingiustizia attraverso il dolore. Costituisce sempre, nell'ultimo degli uomini così come nel Cristo, una protesta impersonale. Ciò che è sacro, lungi dall'essere la persona, è quello che in un essere umano è impersonale. Tutto ciò che nell'uomo è impersonale è sacro, nient'altro lo è. Ciò che è sacro nella scienza è la verità. Ciò che è sacro nell'arte è la bellezza. La verità e la bellezza sono impersonali" In quello sguardo di dolore che si affaccia alla finestra, ignorato e non ricambiato, c'è qualcosa di sacro, c'è l'innocenza ferita, c'è una purezza tradita che conserva, integra, la propria dignità incorruttibile. Dopo qualche ora, un altra sequenza esprime questo profondo e immenso umanesimo, ovvero la carrellata sui volti di questi vagabondi, diseredati e sconfitti dall'esistenza, consumati nell'attesa di interminabili tragitti sotto il freddo più crudele, dilaniati dalla pioggia e dalla miseria esistenziale. La fissità dello sguardo dilata il tempo arrivando a produrre un ipnosi, data dalla sospensione di un presente in cui il passato e il futuro si annullano, e in quella sospensione il crudo realismo scivola nella contemplazione, nella stasi dove la realtà si apre come un fiore e si rivela nel suo volto più profondo e autentico, emerge così la poesia. L'ineffabile che comunica la sacralità dell'impersonale che alberga in ogni umano, la sua indistruttibile dignità. <<Gli sventurati non trovano ascolto, essi sono nella stessa condizione di qualcuno cui fosse stata mozzata la lingua e che a tratti dimenticasse la propria infermità. Le loro labbra si agitano e nessun suono giunge alle orecchie. Proprio perché hanno la certezza di non essere uditi, presto diventano incapaci nell'uso del linguaggio. Tanto la sventura è orrenda quanto l'espressione autentica della sventura è sovranamente bella. Lo splendore della bellezza viene diffuso sulla sventura dalla luce dello spirito di giustizia e amore, il solo che permette a un pensiero umano di guardare e riprodurre la sventura quale è.>> (Simone Weil) Questo è esattamente quello che è riuscito a fare lo sguardo di Bela Tarr, sospendere la realtà nella stasi della contemplazione e, in essa, trovare la luce nei volti sconfitti dell'umanità eternamente vagabonda, quella carrellata con la musica di Mihály Víg sembra riprodurre il moto circolare dei pianeti attorno al sole, poichè il volto è la stella luminosa che sorge e tramonta nell'oscurità dello schermo, il paesaggio eterno dell'interiorità, il principio e la fine di ogni storia. ”Il modo in cui si presenta l’Altro, superando l’idea dell’Altro in me, lo chiamiamo, appunto, volto” (Emmanuel Levinas) Il cinema si riduce tutto a questo, perché infondo guardiamo se non per cercare di trovare noi stessi negli altri? È questo che tenta di fare Estike, prima cercando aiuto al dottore e poi alla folla danzante. Il dottore invece è l'incarnazione di una crisi, quella dello guardo e dell'intelletto che cerca di interpretare ciò che vede, è prigioniero del suo inerte immobilismo, e il suo sguardo è morto, fisso, impossibilitato ad attraversare le barriere delle superfici, incapace di vedere al di là del ristretto perimetro della sua prospettiva (la sequenza della soggettiva attraverso il binocolo) Nel momento in cui deciderà di uscire fuori dal suo guscio di mortifera passività, egli affogherà nell'oscurità della campagna, annegherà nella pioggia proprio nel momento in cui si verificheranno i due eventi più importanti di tutta la vicenda, da una parte l'arrivo di Irimiás e dall'altra la morte di Estike. L'attimo del suo svenimento nella selva oscura è il momento del definitivo fallimento dello sguardo, quella cecità che non sarà in grado di scorgere l'immenso dolore nel volto di Estike, ma che la lascerà andare via, verso la morte. La frammentazione temporale di ogni prospettiva ci farà vedere lo stesso attimo di una medesima sequenza vissuta e percepita da diverse prospettive, così quando noi rivediamo il volto di Estike affacciato alla finestra, sappiamo che lei è già morta. La vediamo solo dopo aver assistito al suo suicidio, il suo sguardo si materializza come quello di un fantasma ormai scomparso e dissipato, ma tenuto vivo, nel calore della sua luce e nella pietà del suo dolore, nel tempo cristallizzato dal cinema, quel tempo immobile in cui vive l'atemporalità della condizione umana. Il dottore non vede oltre il riquadro della sua finestra, è costretto fatalmente nei limiti della propria soggettività, e allora è proprio attraverso lo strumento del cinema (e dell'arte in generale) che si configura la possibilità di poter superare la bidimensionalità di quella finestra, di varcare i limiti della ristrettezza nella nostra percezione. Attraverso il cinema noi possiamo passare direttamente "dall'altra parte", varcare la soglia della nostra percezione individuale per entrare all'interno del cuore dell'altro, e nell'altro arrivare a vedere noi stessi. Non è il guardare passivamente delle persone che scorrono sullo schermo, ma guardare attraverso gli occhi delle persone che sono nello schermo. Allora ecco che quando appare lo sguardo di Estike noi riusciamo a sentire tutta la profonda tragedia che è nel suo cuore, sentiamo quel grido silenzioso e inarticolato che cerca aiuto nel prossimo. Siamo stati prima all'interno della sua prospettiva e poi fuori, all'interno di quel bar in cui si scatena la follia del tango di Satana, nella confusione dei sensi che allontana la disperazione di ogni membro della comunità, nel caos che produce quella cecità che rende Estike solo un fantasma affacciato alla finestra. Nessuno vede, tranne noi, che vediamo, sentiamo e condividiamo la sua disperazione. Il dottore è colui che vede mentre Estike è colei che vorrebbe essere vista, entrambi sono separati dall'altro da una finestra. Allora l'impossibilità di essere visti e l'impossibilità di vedere, viene colmata dalla trascendenza insita nella possibilità dello sguardo cinematografico, che non ha niente a che fare con la mera tecnica, ma con la capacità di sentire profondamente ciò che si vede. Bela Tarr arriva a questa trascendenza in tre momenti distinti ma vicini, e lo fa tutte le volte grazie alla dilatazione temporale nella carrellata. Due uomini stanno parlando faccia a faccia e all'improvviso la m.d.p si allontana in un lungo movimento laterale fermandosi nell'inquadratura fissa di un maiale nel fango, il dettaglio della conversazione viene trasceso e superato dallo sguardo onnipervadente di Tarr, che per mezzo della musica arriva a produrre una stasi poetica, un flusso contemplativo in cui l'interiorità dei personaggi (e la nostra) si fonde con l'esteriorità; dal dettaglio si passa all'insieme e nella lentezza di questo movimento lo sguardo arriva a penetrare il mondo stesso. In questa stasi contemplativa il mondo, come in una rivelazione poetica, pare rivelarsi, dischiudersi e denudarsi da ogni velo. Tutto diventa parte integrante dell'abbraccio di quello sguardo, poiché tutto merita di essere guardato, un filo d'erba soffocato nel fango come un lurido cane dilaniato dalla fame e dalla sporcizia, una pozzanghera di putridume tanto quanto un volto, le vacche e le crepe sopra i muri così come il vento e la pioggia sono la meteria vivente dell'immanenza, di quest'attimo che è qui ed ora, osservato nel proprio puro accadere. Si parte da ciò che è qui ed ora, davanti a noi, come un muro pieno di crepe o un maiale che si abbevera in una pozzanghera, per arrivare a vedere e sentire il flusso continuo che parte da quel singolo movimento per poi dilatarsi ed espandersi, arrivando a pervadere la totalità della realtà. Tutto ciò che è qui e adesso fa parte, nel suo insieme, di un unica ed eterna storia, ecco perché non è importante solo il dialogo che avviene fra due uomini, ma quanto loro è importante ciò che è intorno a loro, poiché la "storia" non si svolge solo nelle righe di un dialogo, la storia è nella totalità del mondo che li avvolge e che li contiene. Pertanto è quella fissità radicale nell'osservazione del mondo a produrre la stasi della contemplazione, in cui il tempo cristallizzato arriva a contenere ciò che trascende il tempo stesso. La continuità spazio-temporale del presente riconduce l'immediatezza del reale ad una purezza assoluta in cui l'immanenza può farsi (e rivelarsi come) territorio della trascendenza. Tutto ciò che è qui e ora finisce per divenire un riflesso nella cui luce abita ciò che è altrove. Questa carrellata verrà ripetuta altre due volte, nel primo caso interromperà di nuovo un dialogo, quello fra Irimiás e altre due persone, per allontanarsi dai corpi e arrivare a sprofondare nella vasta oscurità della Puszta ungherese che, in questo nuovo attimo dilatato non è più un luogo spietatamente concreto, ma è divenuto un paesaggio interiore, lo specchio emotivo della tragedia in cui tutti sono immersi. Nel secondo ed ultimo caso la m.d.p, che osserva i personaggi e ci fa ascoltare i loro dialoghi nella nuova fatiscente dimora, si allontana ancora una volta da quei corpi per dirigersi altrove, verso il volto di un misterioso Gufo ( il simbolo di colui che vede nell'oscurità, portando alla luce ciò che è buio? Proprio come lo sguardo del cinema, che parte dall'oscurità per inseguire ombre di luce ) Si crea pertanto un contrasto tra la forza disgregante del Verbo e del potere ( Irimiás inganna attraverso la parola così come gli ufficiali riscrivono le identità di ogni membro della comunitá per farli diventare meri strumenti sottomessi alla volontà politica, che è sempre e irrimediabilmente perversa ) e quella unificante dell'immagine, della visione poetica che arriva a trascendere le limitazioni di ogni linguaggio, che arriva a farci scorgere la scintilla del nostro io più intimo nell'oscurità del volto dell'Altro, quell'estraneo che, in un improvvisa profusione di empatia diviene quanto di più vicino abbiamo. Filmare i volti per arrivare a scorgere ciò che è oltre i volti, per arrivare a dare forma all'informe e indistruttibile dignità umana, questo è il cinema di Bela Tarr. IL FINALE= Ad ogni passo in avanti ne corrisponde uno indietro, così ritorniamo di nuovo davanti alla finestra del dottore, che ancora crede di vedere e sapere ciò che ha di fronte, ma ormai tutti sono andati via, scomparsi per sempre. Dopo la visione del presagio apocalittico (il vecchio che grida impaurito per l'arrivo dei Turchi) il dottore decide di far finta di non aver visto niente, ma ormai avvolto dalla paura, barrica la finestra della sua casa, e simbolicamente chiude il sipario su una storia che però, nell'esatto momento in cui finisce, si appresta a ricominciare. Perchè in quella primordiale oscurità l'impotenza della sua cecità si riscatta nella possibilità creatrice insita nell'immaginazione, quella dell'affabulazione; lo scrutatore impotente ora diviene demiurgo, il buio ha inghiottito tutte le figure umane, ora è solo possibile immaginarle, e pertanto raccontarle. La storia che racconterà il dottore è Satantango, che come ogni storia che coinvolge l'umanità è ciclica ed eterna, dall'alba dei tempi ad oggi, dall'Antico Testamento ad ora, tutte le storie sono già state raccontate. “Tutto ciò che è diritto mente. Ogni verità è ricurva, il tempo stesso è un cerchio. L’eterna clessidra dell’esistenza viene sempre di nuovo capovolta – e tu con essa, granello di polvere." Primer disclaimer que tuve que averiguar por si le tranquiliza a alguien: Se supone que el gato no fue lastimado, y se le adiestró durante semanas jugando con la niña para llevarse a gusto, los sonidos de dolor y quejido del gato fueron agregados en post producción, y durante la escena de la leche fue sedado y se rodó la escena justo donde se empezaba a dormir, el gato fue adoptado a posteriori por Bela Tarr 😅 Dicho esto ya puedo hablar de la película, evidentemente lo primero que llama la atención son las 7 horas de duración, la película es lenta, lentísima incluso, y hay que tener disposición a verla para entrar en la atmósfera, por lo mismo yo me levanté a las 6 am para poder verla de un tirón, una vez dentro de la película como la mayoría son planos secuencias largos la sensación es de que pasa menos tiempo, la misma película cambia la noción del tiempo con sonidos repetitivos como la campana, el acordeón o un ruido que se escucha de fondo a veces y obviamente busca de forma intencional que el espectador sienta el propio paso del tiempo y creo que lo logra. Respecto a lo que yo interpreto de la película considero que habla sobre la miseria y degeneración de la sociedad y sus propios integrantes en una sociedad rota como la Hungría en la decadencia del comunismo y como no existe una esperanza alguna de cambio o de siquiera recuperar la dignidad, incluso con la llegada mesiánica de Irimías que es más bien un falso profeta de cara a ellos y que realmente los desprecia como se ve en el informe (simbolismo del nuevo “capitalismo” que llega a reemplazar el regimen antigüo?). De la trama se puede decir poco porque realmente pasan pocas cosas, pero la narrativa de como se ven los mismos hechos de distintas perspectivas y se retrocede en el tiempo es exquisita, y de cierta forma conversa con esta atmósfera de que todo es un bucle como sus propias vidas, el final es inconcluso pero es parte de lo que se busca no? Realmente no entendí por qué no se fueron con el dinero inmediatamente, o por qué Irimías tenía ese respeto en la comunidad (evidentemente era más inteligente, pero hizo algo por ellos en el pasado? Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

I tried watching The Turin Horse , and I didn't get anything out of it. So I then listened to Jonathan Rosenbaum's audio commentary. hoping it might offer something I had missed. Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Only after death, if I find myself in hell. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. I come away from this thinking there are two possible reasons for this decision by the filmmaker. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. The cart is before the horse; this man just wants to show us he has the capacity to make a long, slow movie. A massive waste of time.

Toda la película es un hombre levantándose de la cama, comiendo papas y volviéndose a acostar. Hay un trecho enorme de la película donde el hombre solo se la pasa comiéndose unas malditas papas. Más o menos a mitad de película llega un sujeto a la casa y dije: finalmente se dignaron a que pasara algo. I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.

The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

I tried watching The Turin Horse , and I didn't get anything out of it. So I then listened to Jonathan Rosenbaum's audio commentary. hoping it might offer something I had missed. Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Only after death, if I find myself in hell. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. I come away from this thinking there are two possible reasons for this decision by the filmmaker. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. The cart is before the horse; this man just wants to show us he has the capacity to make a long, slow movie. A massive waste of time.

O kadar sene yaşadığı toprağı bir kova su için kimseyle paylaşmayan adam kuyu kurur kurmaz evi bir saniye düşünmeden terk ediyor. Dün “benim" dediği yer bugün hiçbir şey. Kızına bakışı bile sevgi yerine hala iş görüyor mu diye kontrol eder gibi. Her gün aynı döngü uyan, giydir, içki, at, patates ye, camdan bak. At yürümüyor hayat ilerlemiyor ve hem açlar hem de patatesi yemiyorlar yani yaşamak için fiziksel sebep olsada anlam yok. Filmde bu noktaya kadar sahiplik, değer ve anlam tamamen işlev üzerinden kurulmuş. Buraya kadar güzel ama takıldığım yer de tam bu. Film sürekli “her şey değersizleşti, insan içten içe öldü” diyor ama baştan gösterdiği canlı bir değer, tutunulacak bir anlam hiç yok ki yıkımını hissedelim. Karakterlerle bağ kurmak zaten mümkün değil çünkü ortada karakter yok sadece hareket eden bedenler var. Ne hissediyorlar, neyin yasını tutuyorlar, neden yaşıyorla. hiçbir şey açılmıyor. Çöküşü izliyoruz ama çöken bir hayat görmediğimiz için etkisi de olmuyor. Başından beri bitmiş bir dünyayı altı kez tekrar izlemek gibi. At yemiyor, kuyu kuruyor, ışık gidiyor. Bunlar büyük metaforlar gibi girip bırakiyor. Sadece “bak her şey sönüyor” diyor. Eee tamam sönüyor da bu bana ne düşündürüyor? İzleyiciye alan açmakla hiçbir şey kurmamak arasında fark var, bunda ikincisi var. Zaten en başından beri hayat mekanik bir tekrar. Dolayısıyla yok oluş bir çöküş gibi değil uzatılmış bir hiçlik gibi. Tempo meselesine gelirsem evet uzun planlar düşünmek için alan açıyor ama bir noktadan sonra aynı şeyi defalarca izlemek derinlikten çok durağanlık hissi yaratmış. Hareketsizlik de bilinçli bir tercih evet ama bu kadar da amaçsızlık izleyiciyle kurulan bağı zorlamış. Tanrı meselesi de çok kararsız. Tanrınının yok olduğu bir evren yerine terk edilmiş ama hala bir düzen tarafından kapatılan bir dünya hissi var. Bir diğer aklımda kalan soru da zaten başından beri ölü doğmuş bir hayatı izliyorsak bunun çöküşünü neden bu kadar uzun izliyoruz? Unutulmaz mı? Evet. I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.

The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. I come away from this thinking there are two possible reasons for this decision by the filmmaker. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. The cart is before the horse; this man just wants to show us he has the capacity to make a long, slow movie. A massive waste of time.

I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.
